texts.label: A
texts.title: The manager
texts.text: Silence in a meeting is not necessarily agreement. Some colleagues need time to test an idea before speaking, while others may feel that the room has already decided. I now leave a deliberate pause and invite views individually rather than rewarding the fastest voice. The pause can improve a decision by separating a first reaction from a considered objection. It should not become an excuse to postpone a choice indefinitely. The disagreement shows that silence has no single meaning. Its value depends on who can use it, who is expected to tolerate it and what happens when someone finally speaks. The strongest position is not the loudest one; it is the account that recognises what its preferred solution leaves unresolved and explains how visitors, residents or colleagues might respond. This qualification keeps comparison meaningful: each writer offers a preference, but also identifies a cost that a less careful account might ignore.

texts.label: B
texts.title: The designer
texts.text: My best design decisions rarely arrive during discussion. They emerge afterwards, when fragments of other people’s comments have had time to combine. I regard silence as part of the creative process, not as evidence that the meeting failed. Creative silence is productive only when later work returns to the shared problem and becomes a proposal others can question. The disagreement shows that silence has no single meaning. Its value depends on who can use it, who is expected to tolerate it and what happens when someone finally speaks. The strongest position is not the loudest one; it is the account that recognises what its preferred solution leaves unresolved and explains how visitors, residents or colleagues might respond. texts.label: The mediator
texts.title: The mediator
texts.text: Silence can be an active intervention. When two people are arguing, a pause may stop them repeating positions and create room for a different question. It is useful only if the mediator can tolerate the discomfort it produces. A mediator should make the purpose of silence explicit, otherwise the pause may feel like suppression rather than care. The disagreement shows that silence has no single meaning. Its value depends on who can use it, who is expected to tolerate it and what happens when someone finally speaks. The strongest position is not the loudest one; it is the account that recognises what its preferred solution leaves unresolved and explains how visitors, residents or colleagues might respond. texts.label: D
texts.title: The consultant
texts.text: I am cautious about celebrating silence. In some organisations, it reflects a hierarchy in which disagreement carries a career cost. Asking people to speak more is not enough; leaders must show that dissent has consequences they can accept. Leaders who value dissent demonstrate it in decisions, not speeches. People judge safety by what happens after criticism. The disagreement shows that silence has no single meaning. Its value depends on who can use it, who is expected to tolerate it and what happens when someone finally speaks. The strongest position is not the loudest one; it is the account that recognises what its preferred solution leaves unresolved and explains how visitors, residents or colleagues might respond. questions.explanation: The manager notes that quiet colleagues may feel the room has already decided.

questions.explanation: The designer says ideas emerge after comments have had time to combine.
